1	---
2	name: text-audit
3	description: Use to check any human-facing text — README, spec, copy, article — for places a first-time reader stops, then repair them.
4	metadata:
5	  version: 1.0.0
6	---
7	
8	# text-audit — read a text as a stranger, fix where they stop
9	
10	This skill checks whether a stranger understands a text, and repairs the places where they stop.
11	
12	**Where the paths in this file point.** `references/` names a file in this skill's own folder, beside
13	this file. Every other path belongs to the project whose text is under audit. A host project that
14	ships its own mechanical lints may list them in `.text-audit/lints.json`, a list of
15	`{surface, command}` entries this skill runs at Step 1 alongside its own; see "The mechanical lints".
16	
17	A **cold reader** meets the text with no knowledge of its history: no earlier draft, no author's
18	intent, no project background beyond the words on the page. A cold reader is a fresh session — one
19	conversation with a model started empty, holding no project skills or rules. By hand it is a person
20	who has not read the text before.
21	
22	An author cannot be their own cold reader: the author holds the context the text is missing, and reads
23	a meaning a stranger cannot reach. This skill supplies the prompt that turns a fresh session, or a
24	person, into that stranger, at [`references/reader-prompt.md`](references/reader-prompt.md).
25	
26	The reading step runs two cold readers over the same text every time. One works under the printed
27	rule list at [`references/reader-prompt.md`](references/reader-prompt.md); one works under
28	[`references/unprompted-reader-brief.md`](references/unprompted-reader-brief.md), which hands over
29	only the text, the reader it is written for, and the task.
30	
31	This skill runs on any text a person will read: a spec section, a README, a decision page, marketing
32	copy, an article, a release note. The loop came from a comprehension gate its author built into a
33	spec-format pipeline: fresh cold readers found new blocking terms on every pass, and terms already
34	repaired stayed repaired, until two reads in a row returned nothing that blocks. Every reading is
35	written to a dated **reading record**, kept beside the audited text or under a project's own record
36	directory: one reading's full output, every stop it reported, and any check that did not run.
37	
38	## The roles and the words this skill uses
39	
40	Three roles run through this skill; two readers fill the cold reader role in every round. One person
41	may hold the auditor role and own the text, and the cold reader is never either of them.
42	
43	- **the auditor** — the session running this skill. It runs the lints, briefs both cold readers,
44	  merges what they return, and writes the fixes.
45	- **the cold reader** — the fresh reader defined above. It reports where it stopped, and repairs
46	  nothing.
47	- **the prompted reader** — a cold reader working under `references/reader-prompt.md`.
48	- **the unprompted reader** — a cold reader holding the text, the reader it is written for, and the
49	  task, at `references/unprompted-reader-brief.md`.
50	- **the person** — whoever owns the text and answers for its intent.
51	
52	A **surface** is a kind of text; this skill covers six — a spec body, human prose, chat, a published
53	artifact, a commit message, and a worker brief. The auditor names the text's one primary surface (an
54	externally-published text also carries the artifact surface), and every rule binding either surface is
55	in force. A README, a report, a decision page, and a skill body stand on human prose; marketing copy
56	and an article stand on the artifact surface; a numbered requirement stands on the spec body (see
57	"Running it on a spec section").
58	
59	The **register** of a surface is the writing rules its text is held to — which words it takes, which
60	sentence shapes, how it addresses its reader, and its word cap: 25 words for a human-prose sentence, 35
61	for a spec-body criterion. The human-prose register this skill ships with is printed at
62	[`references/human-prose-rules.md`](references/human-prose-rules.md); a host project may keep a fuller
63	rule home and point `.text-audit/lints.json` at it, and where it does not, the bundled rules are the
64	whole set.
65	
66	A **class** is the shape of a mistake: the form it takes wherever it turns up. One rule names one
67	class, and a stop in one place stands for that class everywhere else.
68	
69	## When it fires
70	
71	Load this skill when a human-facing text is about to ship and its clarity matters: a README before a
72	push, a spec section after an edit, a decision page before it goes to the person, a piece of marketing
73	copy or an article draft. The trigger is a person asking whether a reader will understand the text:
74	"audit this", "cold-read this", "is this clear", "will a stranger get this".
75	
76	## Work that belongs elsewhere
77	
78	- **A design review of a spec** judges the design behind the words — whether similar features behave
79	  one way, and which same-kind items the spec left ungrouped. This skill reads whether the words land
80	  on a stranger and invents no answer about the design; run both for the failures only each finds.
81	- **An argument with a spec's claims** hunts a missing state, a false invariant, and an unhandled
82	  transition. This skill reads the words, and judges no claim the spec makes.
83	- **Taste and voice** stay with the person and whatever writing skills the host installs beside this
84	  one. This skill holds a text to the register of its surface and reports where a reader stops; it
85	  grades no voice and rewrites no style beyond those rules.
86	- **Machine-read text** needs no cold reader, because no stranger returns to it: a worker brief, a
87	  checkpoint, an internal note.
88	
89	## The loop
90	
91	The audit runs in five steps. A **reading round** is one pass by each of the two readers, and both
92	readers of a round are **cheap readers**: a fresh session holding no project skills or rules, only this
93	skill's own prompt and the text. The audit closes when both readers of a round return zero blocking
94	findings, in two consecutive rounds.
95	
96	1. **Run the mechanical lints, and fix every hit.** Run every check a script or a grep can decide
97	   before a reader spends attention on the text, and fix each hit at this step — see "The mechanical
98	   lints". The cold readers then spend their attention on what no script can judge.
99	2. **Hand the text to two fresh cold readers.** Both sessions hold zero context on the text's history.
100	   One works under the reader-prompt, one under the unprompted reader's brief; the two run apart, and
101	   neither sees the other's output. Each returns the places a stranger stops, each marked blocking or
102	   non-blocking, and repairs nothing. Where the text leaves an answer out, that session writes down the
103	   guess it made in place of a missing answer, showing where the text sent the reader.
104	3. **The auditor merges the two lists**, alone, in this order: read both lists whole before matching
105	   anything; match stops naming the same passage (the two readers label a passage differently, so match
106	   on the passage each stop quotes); mark a passage both readers stopped on as found by both — those
107	   stops lead the list; where the two readers named different faults in one passage, keep both faults
108	   under that entry; keep every stop one reader found alone, recording which reader found it; carry
109	   every stop into one ordered list — both-found first, then the remaining blocking stops, then the
110	   non-blocking ones. Before step 4, the auditor checks each stop's factual claims against the sources
111	   it cites and cuts what no source holds (refutation) — itself, or a second worker told to knock each
112	   stop down. That merged list is what step 4 repairs, and the reading record carries it whole.
113	4. **Write each fix from the source.** For a blocking finding, take the fix from the material the text
114	   already rests on — see "Where a fix comes from". A non-blocking finding waits for the person's taste
115	   call once the blocking ones are gone.
116	5. **Read again, and close on two clean rounds.** After the fixes land, hand the text to a fresh pair
117	   of readers, one under each brief. **A repair writes text nobody has read** — both readers of round
118	   one met the text as it stood before the fixes, so neither could have caught a defect inside the
119	   repair's own new sentences. Round two is the round that earns the closing: an audit stopped after
120	   round one has shipped text nobody met. Say so in the reading record when a run stops early, and
121	   record the audit as open.
122	
123	A section-sized run puts one definition and a handful of sentences in front of a reader; a whole-page
124	run puts every sentence of that page in front of one reader. Audit the section the edit touched, and
125	read a whole page when the person asks for it.
126	
127	## Running it on a spec section
128	
129	A spec section is one requirement with its Context paragraph, its User Story, and its acceptance
130	criteria (a short run of such requirements counts too); ten requirements, about 250 lines, is a working
131	size a fresh reader holds without a repair breaking a requirement far away. Three things differ from a
132	human-prose run: a requirement-shape lint applies — context before criteria, one trigger and one
133	response per criterion, every judgment naming a judge and a measure (declare a script for it in
134	`.text-audit/lints.json`, or read by hand); a criterion writes in the third person while its Context
135	paragraph speaks to the reader directly, so neither judges the other's sentences; and every mark a
136	machine reads — a requirement's number, its anchors, a phrase a test quotes — must survive the repair
137	unchanged, since moving one can break a host's own tests or generated indexes. A fix comes from the
138	spec's own neighbours — architecture, the recorded decision, the test matrix; where none answers, the
139	finding is a real hole and takes an inline `[GAP: what is missing]` note. Run a host's own test suite
140	or structure checks after the repair, alongside the meaning-check reader below; where none are
141	declared, say in the reading record that they did not run.
142	
143	## The mechanical lints
144	
145	Run these before any reader. Each names the class it catches and a grep fallback needing no script. A
146	host project may declare its own script for any of these classes, or one of its own, in
147	`.text-audit/lints.json` as `{surface, command}` entries, each command taking the audited file's path
148	as its last argument; run every declared command whose surface matches the text's own before falling
149	back to grep.
150	
151	- **Every term is defined at first use.** A domain noun — one whose meaning is particular to this
152	  project or field — carries a one-sentence definition before its first working use.
153	    - Grep fallback: list capitalized and coined nouns, and confirm each has an introducing sentence

description: Use to check any human-facing text — README, spec, copy, article — for places a first-time reader stops, then repair them.
metadata:
  version: 1.0.0
---

# text-audit — read a text as a stranger, fix where they stop

This skill checks whether a stranger understands a text, and repairs the places where they stop.

**Where the paths in this file point.** `references/` names a file in this skill's own folder, beside
this file. Every other path belongs to the project whose text is under audit. A host project that
ships its own mechanical lints may list them in `.text-audit/lints.json`, a list of
`{surface, command}` entries this skill runs at Step 1 alongside its own; see "The mechanical lints".

A **cold reader** meets the text with no knowledge of its history: no earlier draft, no author's
intent, no project background beyond the words on the page. A cold reader is a fresh session — one
conversation with a model started empty, holding no project skills or rules. By hand it is a person
who has not read the text before.

An author cannot be their own cold reader: the author holds the context the text is missing, and reads
a meaning a stranger cannot reach. This skill supplies the prompt that turns a fresh session, or a
person, into that stranger, at [`references/reader-prompt.md`](references/reader-prompt.md).

The reading step runs two cold readers over the same text every time. One works under the printed
rule list at [`references/reader-prompt.md`](references/reader-prompt.md); one works under
[`references/unprompted-reader-brief.md`](references/unprompted-reader-brief.md), which hands over
only the text, the reader it is written for, and the task.

This skill runs on any text a person will read: a spec section, a README, a decision page, marketing
copy, an article, a release note. The loop came from a comprehension gate its author built into a
spec-format pipeline: fresh cold readers found new blocking terms on every pass, and terms already
repaired stayed repaired, until two reads in a row returned nothing that blocks. Every reading is
written to a dated **reading record**, kept beside the audited text or under a project's own record
directory: one reading's full output, every stop it reported, and any check that did not run.

## The roles and the words this skill uses

Three roles run through this skill; two readers fill the cold reader role in every round. One person
may hold the auditor role and own the text, and the cold reader is never either of them.

- **the auditor** — the session running this skill. It runs the lints, briefs both cold readers,
  merges what they return, and writes the fixes.
- **the cold reader** — the fresh reader defined above. It reports where it stopped, and repairs
  nothing.
- **the prompted reader** — a cold reader working under `references/reader-prompt.md`.
- **the unprompted reader** — a cold reader holding the text, the reader it is written for, and the
  task, at `references/unprompted-reader-brief.md`.
- **the person** — whoever owns the text and answers for its intent.

A **surface** is a kind of text; this skill covers six — a spec body, human prose, chat, a published
artifact, a commit message, and a worker brief. The auditor names the text's one primary surface (an
externally-published text also carries the artifact surface), and every rule binding either surface is
in force. A README, a report, a decision page, and a skill body stand on human prose; marketing copy
and an article stand on the artifact surface; a numbered requirement stands on the spec body (see
"Running it on a spec section").

The **register** of a surface is the writing rules its text is held to — which words it takes, which
sentence shapes, how it addresses its reader, and its word cap: 25 words for a human-prose sentence, 35
for a spec-body criterion. The human-prose register this skill ships with is printed at
[`references/human-prose-rules.md`](references/human-prose-rules.md); a host project may keep a fuller
rule home and point `.text-audit/lints.json` at it, and where it does not, the bundled rules are the
whole set.

A **class** is the shape of a mistake: the form it takes wherever it turns up. One rule names one
class, and a stop in one place stands for that class everywhere else.

## When it fires

Load this skill when a human-facing text is about to ship and its clarity matters: a README before a
push, a spec section after an edit, a decision page before it goes to the person, a piece of marketing
copy or an article draft. The trigger is a person asking whether a reader will understand the text:
"audit this", "cold-read this", "is this clear", "will a stranger get this".

## Work that belongs elsewhere

- **A design review of a spec** judges the design behind the words — whether similar features behave
  one way, and which same-kind items the spec left ungrouped. This skill reads whether the words land
  on a stranger and invents no answer about the design; run both for the failures only each finds.
- **An argument with a spec's claims** hunts a missing state, a false invariant, and an unhandled
  transition. This skill reads the words, and judges no claim the spec makes.
- **Taste and voice** stay with the person and whatever writing skills the host installs beside this
  one. This skill holds a text to the register of its surface and reports where a reader stops; it
  grades no voice and rewrites no style beyond those rules.
- **Machine-read text** needs no cold reader, because no stranger returns to it: a worker brief, a
  checkpoint, an internal note.

## The loop

The audit runs in five steps. A **reading round** is one pass by each of the two readers, and both
readers of a round are **cheap readers**: a fresh session holding no project skills or rules, only this
skill's own prompt and the text. The audit closes when both readers of a round return zero blocking
findings, in two consecutive rounds.

1. **Run the mechanical lints, and fix every hit.** Run every check a script or a grep can decide
   before a reader spends attention on the text, and fix each hit at this step — see "The mechanical
   lints". The cold readers then spend their attention on what no script can judge.
2. **Hand the text to two fresh cold readers.** Both sessions hold zero context on the text's history.
   One works under the reader-prompt, one under the unprompted reader's brief; the two run apart, and
   neither sees the other's output. Each returns the places a stranger stops, each marked blocking or
   non-blocking, and repairs nothing. Where the text leaves an answer out, that session writes down the
   guess it made in place of a missing answer, showing where the text sent the reader.
3. **The auditor merges the two lists**, alone, in this order: read both lists whole before matching
   anything; match stops naming the same passage (the two readers label a passage differently, so match
   on the passage each stop quotes); mark a passage both readers stopped on as found by both — those
   stops lead the list; where the two readers named different faults in one passage, keep both faults
   under that entry; keep every stop one reader found alone, recording which reader found it; carry
   every stop into one ordered list — both-found first, then the remaining blocking stops, then the
   non-blocking ones. Before step 4, the auditor checks each stop's factual claims against the sources
   it cites and cuts what no source holds (refutation) — itself, or a second worker told to knock each
   stop down. That merged list is what step 4 repairs, and the reading record carries it whole.
4. **Write each fix from the source.** For a blocking finding, take the fix from the material the text
   already rests on — see "Where a fix comes from". A non-blocking finding waits for the person's taste
   call once the blocking ones are gone.
5. **Read again, and close on two clean rounds.** After the fixes land, hand the text to a fresh pair
   of readers, one under each brief. **A repair writes text nobody has read** — both readers of round
   one met the text as it stood before the fixes, so neither could have caught a defect inside the
   repair's own new sentences. Round two is the round that earns the closing: an audit stopped after
   round one has shipped text nobody met. Say so in the reading record when a run stops early, and
   record the audit as open.

A section-sized run puts one definition and a handful of sentences in front of a reader; a whole-page
run puts every sentence of that page in front of one reader. Audit the section the edit touched, and
read a whole page when the person asks for it.

## Running it on a spec section

A spec section is one requirement with its Context paragraph, its User Story, and its acceptance
criteria (a short run of such requirements counts too); ten requirements, about 250 lines, is a working

human-prose run: a requirement-shape lint applies — context before criteria, one trigger and one
response per criterion, every judgment naming a judge and a measure (declare a script for it in
`.text-audit/lints.json`, or read by hand); a criterion writes in the third person while its Context
paragraph speaks to the reader directly, so neither judges the other's sentences; and every mark a
machine reads — a requirement's number, its anchors, a phrase a test quotes — must survive the repair
unchanged, since moving one can break a host's own tests or generated indexes. A fix comes from the
spec's own neighbours — architecture, the recorded decision, the test matrix; where none answers, the
finding is a real hole and takes an inline `[GAP: what is missing]` note. Run a host's own test suite
or structure checks after the repair, alongside the meaning-check reader below; where none are
declared, say in the reading record that they did not run.

as its last argument; run every declared command whose surface matches the text's own before falling

      above its first use.
- **A weak relational word fills the slot it opens.** Words such as *depends*, *related*, *handles*,

      reader reports a new slot-opening word, add it to the host's own word list, or to this skill's
      working copy where none exists.

    - Grep fallback: list each named thing, and confirm one name carries it throughout.

carrying two meanings, a sentence with no actor, an image with no referent. **The unprompted reader**

reader alone, against a two-fifths-to-a-third share of stops that a refutation pass throws out.

judging work than one reader alone — expect a sizeable share of what either returns to fall away under
refutation — and that cost is what buys the coverage neither reader gets alone.

1	# The rules a human-prose audit holds a text to
2	
3	This file belongs to the `text-audit` skill, whose body is [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md). That body
4	defines a surface and a register, and it says when a text is held to the rules below.
5	
6	The rules below are the whole set a human-prose audit holds a text to. They are edited in one file,
7	`guardrails/language-rules.json`, in the live-spec repository.
8	
9	`scripts/gen-language-consumers.py` builds four artifacts from that one file:
10	
11	- the writer's page, `docs/language-rules.md`;
12	- the maintainer's page, `docs/language-rule-coverage.md`;
13	- the rule text the judging model reads, `hooks/language-laws.json`;
14	- the block below.
15	
16	Two of those pages carry more than this sheet does. `docs/language-rules.md` gives each rule with its
17	examples, its exceptions, and its thresholds. `docs/language-worked-example.md` walks one short document
18	end to end against these rules, and names the rule at each fix.
19	
20	<!-- generated:human-prose-rules — scripts/gen-language-consumers.py owns the block below -->
21	
22	## The rules this audit holds human prose to
23	
24	Every rule below binds human prose, which is text a person reads to understand something or to decide something. A README, a decision page, a report, a skill's own body, and a documentation page carry it. So do the prose paragraphs inside a spec. A documentation page carries `artifact` as well once it is published outside the project.
25	
26	This block prints 50 of the 66 rules the source carries. A code missing from the run below belongs to a rule binding other surfaces only, or to a retired rule whose code left the set. A rule binding human prose may also bind chat, a commit message, or a worker brief. Its recorded case may come from one of those surfaces.
27	
28	They are printed here out of `guardrails/language-rules.json`, which is where each one is edited. A change made in this block is overwritten by the next run of `scripts/gen-language-consumers.py`.
29	
30	Each entry names the class of mistake, states the rule, gives the question to ask of a sentence, and carries one recorded case under it. The case shows written text on the left. The right side shows its repair, or an instruction where the repair depends on facts the case does not carry. Every case the class was built from lives in the rule home.
31	
32	- **an ordinary word carrying a private project meaning** (`r01`)
33	  A word keeps its everyday meaning. A term this project needs holds one glossary entry, written in plain words. The body then uses that term unchanged, with no definition attached.
34	  *Ask:* Would a person outside this project recognize this word, or does the text gloss it in plain words where it first appears?
35	    - `The system shall red a branch whose merge-base sits behind main's tip.` → `The system shall refuse a branch whose merge-base sits behind main's tip.`
36	- **a coined, loan-translated, or respelled word standing where a plain standard word exists** (`r02`)
37	  Where the industry has a word, the text writes the industry's word. A term this project coined is replaced by the standard word, or defined where it first appears. In the reader's own language, a term is written as a real word of that language.
38	  *Ask:* Does a standard word already name this thing? Is the word used here that standard word, written as a real word of the reader's own language?
39	    - `the door` → `the entry point`
40	- **a name stacking two nouns with no relation between them** (`r03`)
41	  A name holds one noun. Where two nouns belong together, a verb or a preposition between them carries the relation.
42	  *Ask:* Does this name run two nouns together, and can a reader say how the second relates to the first?
43	    - `chat-law reminder` → `the reminder that carries the chat laws`
44	- **one thing answering to a second name** (`r04`)
45	  One thing carries one name in every sentence, from its first use onward.
46	  *Ask:* Does any thing named here appear under a different word somewhere else in this document or its neighbours?
47	    - `the mechanical checks, in the README, for the step the skill body calls the mechanical lints` → `the mechanical lints, in both places`
48	- **a predicate applied to a subject that cannot carry it** (`r05`)
49	  A verb or an adjective attaches to a subject that can carry it. Where the subject cannot act, the sentence names the actor that can: a person, a script, a hook, or a model.
50	  *Ask:* Can the thing this sentence names as its subject perform this verb, or hold this quality?
51	    - `the numbers do not show red` → `name the actor that shows a colour, or state what the numbers do`
52	- **a number standing with no ground** (`r06`)
53	  Every number says what it counts, what it is compared against, and which direction is better. A number chosen rather than derived says that it was chosen.
54	  *Ask:* Can a reader say what this number is measured against and which way is better?
55	    - `the register targets 15-25 words, and a sentence past ~25 words is a hit` → `a sentence stays between 15 and 25 words, and one past 25 is a hit`
56	- **a set pointed at by a count, a pointer, or a position, with its members never given** (`r07`)
57	  A sentence that depends on a set gives that set, or points by name to the one place holding it. A part of a set is named by what its members are.
58	  *Ask:* Can a person who reads this sentence alone name the members of the set it points at?
59	    - `**Case: the three legs**` → `**Case: the prototype-reference leg, the completeness scan, and the behaviour-traces-to-spec check**`
60	- **a sentence running past the word cap for its surface** (`r08`)
61	  A sentence stays under the word cap for its surface.
62	  *Ask:* Does this sentence stay under the cap for its surface?
63	- **a text breaking a rule it states** (`r09`)
64	  A text ships once it obeys every rule it states. The sentence stating a rule is the first place to check that rule.
65	  *Ask:* Does the sentence stating this rule obey the rule it states?
66	    - `a 62-word sentence inside the file that states the 25-word cap` → `the same rule in three sentences, the longest of them 41 words`
67	- **a thing named by denying its neighbour** (`r10`)
68	  A sentence says what a thing is, in its own words. A boundary worth naming gets its own plain sentence.
69	  *Ask:* Does the denied half give the reader anything the reader did not already have?
70	    - `X, not Y` → `Say what the thing IS in its own sentence`
71	- **an internal code leading a sentence to the reader** (`r11`)
72	  Plain words carry the meaning, and an internal code trails. In chat the code sits in parentheses at the sentence's end. In a document it sits in square brackets at the line's end.
73	  *Ask:* Does the sentence still carry its meaning with the code removed, and does the code stand anywhere other than at the end?
74	    - `INV-141 gives the design review a pass of its own.` → `The design review runs as a pass of its own [INV-141].`
75	- **a word grading how important or how good a thing is** (`r12`)
76	  A text states what a thing is or does, and lets the reader weigh it. A word grading importance or quality stands only beside a concrete fact.
77	  *Ask:* Does this sentence tell the reader how much to care about what it reports?
78	    - `Two constraints, and they are hard ones.` → `Two constraints.`
79	- **a sentence grading the person, or grading the writer's own act** (`r13`)
80	  A remark from the person is answered, and the answer says what follows from it. A text lets its own honesty and rigour show through what it reports.
81	  *Ask:* Does this sentence carry a fact, or a verdict on the person's remark or on the writer's own work?
82	    - `good question` → `answer it, and say what follows from the answer`
83	- **a sentence carrying no information** (`r14`)
84	  Every sentence shown to the person advances the finding, the decision, or the action. A sentence carrying a fact the reader would otherwise lose stays, however short.
85	  *Ask:* Does the reader do anything differently because this sentence is here?
86	    - `Its whole job is to mark where it stopped, what it guessed, and why.` → `deleted, since the two sentences above it already say this`
87	- **a word inflating a statement while adding nothing** (`r15`)
88	  A word earns its place by adding information. A phrase whose deletion changes nothing is deleted.
89	  *Ask:* Does removing this word change what the sentence says?
90	    - `really` → `delete`
91	- **the language each surface is written in** (`r18`)
92	  Documents, commits, code, and artifacts are written in English, and conversation runs in the human's pinned language.
93	  *Ask:* Is this text in the language its surface is pinned to?
94	    - `a commit message in Russian, in a repository whose documents are pinned to English` → `the message in English, with the conversation about it staying Russian`
95	- **English that reads as compressed or poetic** (`r20`)
96	  English in a document or an artifact reads like a native technical writer: short subject-verb-object sentences, common words, and no poetic compression.
97	  *Ask:* Could a native technical writer have written this sentence for an open-source project?
98	    - `the sketch itself carries the look` → `name the actor and say plainly what it does`
99	- **a word standing in all capitals** (`r23`)
100	  Every word is written in ordinary case. Force comes from the declarative statement itself.
101	  *Ask:* Is this word in capitals because it is a name the project has defined, or to make the sentence louder?
102	    - `CHANGES` → `changes`
103	- **the person an explanatory sentence speaks in** (`r25`)
104	  Explanatory text addresses the reader as `you` for what a person does, and names the component for what software does.
105	  *Ask:* Does this sentence tell the reader what they do, in words spoken to them?
106	    - `one` → `you`
107	- **a sentence with no actor, or its action buried in a noun** (`r26`)
108	  A rule sentence says who does what and when, in the active voice with a named actor. Its action lives in a verb.
109	  *Ask:* Does this sentence answer who does this, to what, and when? Does its action live in a verb?
110	    - `the verification of the claim occurs` → `the suite verifies the claim`
111	- **an opener saying what a thing is not** (`r27`)
112	  A sentence opens with what a thing is.
113	  *Ask:* Does the opening clause say what the thing is before it says what it is not?
114	    - `It doesn't know what a PRD is. It knows entities, states, transitions, invariants.` → `It works from entities, states, transitions, and invariants, rather than from a document's genre.`
115	- **a judgment with no judge and no measure** (`r32`)
116	  Every judgment names its judge and its inputs.
117	  *Ask:* Who decides whether this is true, and by what measure?
118	    - `broken` → `name the judge and the measure`
119	- **a relational word leaving its slot empty** (`r33`)
120	  A relational word fills every slot it opens, right where the word stands.
121	  *Ask:* Relative to what, by what measure, or else what alternative?
122	    - `a few` → `state the exact quantity`
123	- **a pronoun with no antecedent in its own sentence** (`r39`)
124	  `it`, `this`, and `they` stand with an unambiguous antecedent in the same sentence. Where none stands, the noun is repeated.
125	  *Ask:* Can a reader say which thing this pronoun points at without looking back a sentence?
126	    - `It returns the places a stranger stops.` → `That session returns the places a stranger stops.`
127	- **an example restating a rule that was already clear** (`r41`)
128	  An example earns its place by resolving an ambiguity, and it uses realistic values. One worked case per rule is enough.
129	  *Ask:* Could a reader have read this rule two ways without this example? Does this example stand in prose, outside a rule entry in the rule home?
130	    - `Grep fallback: read for the four classes by hand - sentences past ~25 words, all-capital words used for emphasis, denial frames, and adjectives that grade a result's size.` → `Grep fallback: read for those four classes by hand. The last one shows up as big, huge, minor, or breakthrough.`
131	- **an abstraction standing where a concrete noun would do** (`r43`)
132	  The text prefers the concrete noun. A required abstraction is grounded with a two- or three-item example at its first use.
133	  *Ask:* Can the reader picture the thing this noun names?
134	    - `an entity` → `A screen, a panel, a saved file`
135	- **a paragraph carrying more than one point** (`r44`)
136	  One paragraph carries one point, stated in its first sentence, with the rest supporting it.
137	  *Ask:* Does a reader who reads only the first sentences of this section still follow it?
138	    - `one paragraph carrying the author's blindness, three example defects, and the loop's origin` → `the author's blindness in its own paragraph, the three defects as a list, and the origin in a paragraph after them`
139	- **a long flat run of peer items at one level** (`r45`)
140	  A document is a tree of grouped topics, and its levels nest without skipping. A long run of peer items is gathered under headed parents.
141	  *Ask:* Does this level hold a run of peer items with no grouping over them?
142	    - `a bullet running the rule, its script, and its grep fallback together in one paragraph` → `the rule as the bullet, with the script and the grep fallback nested under it`
143	- **a reply that buries its answer** (`r46`)
144	  A reply opens with the answer: the outcome, the decision, or the finding. The opening runs a few lines, and the reader may stop there. Reasoning, evidence, and options stand underneath.
145	  *Ask:* Can the reader stop after the opening block and still hold the answer?
146	    - `a report opening with the method it ran, and the finding in its last paragraph` → `the finding in the opening lines, and the method underneath it`
147	- **an offer to do work the writer could already derive** (`r48`)
148	  A derivable act is done and reported done. A backlog item is parked for the human only after a fresh test of whether the answer can be derived now.
149	  *Ask:* Does this sentence offer to do something the writer already has everything to do?
150	    - `just say the word` → `do the act and report it done`
151	- **a mistake expanded into a self-audit paragraph** (`r49`)
152	  A mistake is owned in one line and fixed.
153	  *Ask:* Does this passage explain the writer's own failure at more length than the fix takes?
154	    - `Direct answer: yes, I broke the method... (a paragraph auditing my own failure)` → `name the fix in one line, make it, and go on`
155	- **a working note handed to the reader unmarked, or a choice with no open answer** (`r50`)
156	  Dense working notes are marked so the reader can skip them, and they carry one idea per line. Every choice offered leaves room for a free-form answer.
157	  *Ask:* Can the reader tell at a glance which lines are notes, and can they answer outside the options given?
158	    - `a dense working note handed to the reader with no mark on it` → `the same note opening with a marker that says it is a working note, one idea per line`
159	- **a task subject written in machine words** (`r52`)
160	  The harness task panel on the human's screen speaks plain product words in the documents' language, understandable at a glance.
161	  *Ask:* Does a person glancing at this task subject know what is being done?
162	    - `run gen-language-consumers.py and splice AUDIT_SKILL_REL` → `print the writing rules into the audit skill`
163	- **human-facing prose drafted by a writer holding the project's own vocabulary** (`r53`)
164	  The first draft of prose a human will read is written by a fresh writer with no package rules loaded, working from a plain brief. The brief states the facts, names the intended reader, and lists the rules binding the surface. A person who has read the rulebook then reviews and revises that draft.
165	  *Ask:* Was this sentence first written by someone who had never read this project's skills, working from a brief?
166	    - `a paragraph drafted by the session that held the whole pack loaded` → `the paragraph drafted by a fresh writer from a plain brief, then revised by someone who has read the rules`
167	- **a changed section shipped before two clean cold readings** (`r54`)
168	  A changed section is read by fresh readers who carry no project context, until two consecutive reads return zero blocking findings. `skills/text-audit/SKILL.md` defines a blocking finding.
169	  *Ask:* Did a reader with no project context read this section and stop nowhere?
170	    - `a section shipped after one reading that returned five stops` → `the section read again after the repairs, and shipped once two readings in a row returned nothing that blocks`
171	- **one fact stated a second time in another place** (`r56`)
172	  One fact lives in one home. Every other place points at that home.
173	  *Ask:* Does another place in this project already state this fact?
174	    - `the writing rules written out a second time inside another skill` → `the rules in one file, and the second skill pointing at that file`
175	- **a phrase the human cut returning in a later draft** (`r57`)
176	  A phrasing the human cut in a review round stays out of every later draft of that artifact. An approved text takes exactly the correction the human named.
177	  *Ask:* Has the human already cut this wording from this artifact?
178	    - `«X — not Y» returning in a later draft, after the human cut it` → `the sentence saying what the thing is, in its own words`
179	- **a defect recorded as examples with no class behind them** (`r61`)
180	  When a text stops a reader, the writer names the class of mistake, defines it, and enters that class in the rule home. The examples under an entry are the recorded evidence that produced the class.
181	  *Ask:* Does the entry state what the mistake is, so a writer can find an instance nobody has met yet?
182	    - `a list of banned words: leg, goes red, station, door` → `the class - a coined word standing where a standard word exists - with those four as its recorded evidence`
183	- **a sentence open to two readings, or hiding its cause or what it leaves out** (`r62`)
184	  A reader reaches one interpretation of a sentence, sees what causes what, and can tell what the text leaves out.
185	  *Ask:* Can a reader read this sentence one way only, name what it makes happen, and say which alternatives it passed over?
186	    - `it hands the text to a fresh reader who has no knowledge of its history and marks every place a stranger stops` → `it hands the text to a fresh reader who knows nothing of its history, and that reader marks every place a stranger stops`
187	- **a thing named by its number, so the reader must leave the sentence to learn what it is** (`r63`)
188	  A sentence names a thing by what it is, and its number trails at the line's end.
189	  *Ask:* Does this sentence say what the thing is? Does it give only a number, a position, or a count the reader must go and resolve?
190	    - `Requirement 233 states the orchestration laws.` → `The requirement on how work is routed between tiers states the orchestration laws [INV-241].`
191	- **parallel items run together inside one sentence** (`r64`)
192	  Two or more parallel items become a bulleted or numbered list under a one-line lead, one item per line.
193	  *Ask:* Does this sentence run several items together where a list would put one on each line?
194	    - `The system shall refuse a branch behind main's tip, a lane with no open row, a host with no worktree line, and a lane past the cap.` → `The system shall refuse each of the four faults below. - a branch behind main's tip; - a lane with no open row; - a host with no worktree line; - a lane past the cap.`
195	- **a rare word standing where an everyday word says the same thing** (`r65`)
196	  A sentence takes the everyday word wherever an everyday word carries the meaning. A rare or bookish word stands only where no everyday word says the same thing. A term of the profession stays as it is, and the words around it come down.
197	  *Ask:* Would a professional reader whose first language is other than English reach for a dictionary on this word?
198	    - `a writer marinated in this project's own vocabulary` → `a writer who has already read this project's rules`
199	- **a document written in the register of the message that asked for it** (`r66`)
200	  The register of a request settles nothing about the register of the document. A person writes a request however is fastest for them. Every document is written to the rules of its surface, whatever the request looked like.
201	  *Ask:* Did this sentence take its tone from the message that asked for the work?
202	    - `ok so the gate basically checks the counts and yells when something is off` → `The gate measures every live document and refuses a push where a count stands above its record.`
203	- **a defined term standing in a file that is read apart from its definition** (`r67`)
204	  A term defined in one home stands in another file only where that file gives its reader a path to the definition. A file read on its own carries the terms it uses, or it names where each one is defined.
205	  *Ask:* Reading this file alone, could I reach the definition of this term?
206	    - `together with the settings ladder` → `together with the four scopes that settle a setting: the session's live word, the host profile, the personal profile, and the package default`
207	- **a placeholder word standing where the thing's own name fits** (`r68`)
208	  A sentence carries the name of the thing it is about. A pronoun or a general word stands only where the name would clutter the sentence. A status word stands only where the sentence has already stated the condition behind it.
209	  *Ask:* Does this word name the thing, or does the reader have to carry the name in from an earlier sentence?
210	    - `This keeps the leading context clear enough to hold the campaign.` → `The leading session then holds enough room to carry the campaign.`
211	- **a step naming a check, a file, or an act with no way to run it or find it** (`r69`)
212	  A step the reader has to carry out names the command that runs it, or the path that holds it. Where the text can name neither, it says so and names what the reader does instead.
213	  *Ask:* Could a reader carry out this step from the page alone, with nothing else on hand?
214	    - `the structure checks over requirement shape, the generated index, the matrix references, and the frozen baseline` → `each of the four checks on its own line, with the command that runs it`
215	- **a set claimed whole while the text carries members outside it, or leaves members out with no reason** (`r70`)
216	  A claim that a set is complete states what the set covers and what it leaves out. The list printed under such a claim carries every member the claim names.
217	  *Ask:* Does the text's own list agree with the claim made over it?
218	    - `These are every rule binding human-prose.` → `the rules binding human prose, with the printed count and the reason a code is missing`
219	- **a claim resting on ground the reader of the page cannot reach** (`r71`)
220	  A claim carries its ground on the page that makes it. A file named beside the claim holds the record, and the page still states what the reader needs.
221	  *Ask:* Can a reader holding this page alone see what this claim rests on?
222	    - `The loop came from the spec-format comprehension gate.` → `what that gate observed, stated on the page, with the file that records it named beside it`
223	- **a number stated without the four parts a measurement carries** (`r72`)
224	  A number stated to a reader carries four things. They are why it is measured, what changes when it moves, its unit, and the method behind it. The four stand in the number's own sentence or in the paragraph around it. A number quoted from a named source inherits that source's method.
225	  *Ask:* Reading this number alone, do I know what is counted, which decision it informs, and which command gives it again?
226	    - `A reading returned fifteen stops.` → `name the unit, the decision the count informs, what changes when it moves, and the command behind it`
227	- **a sentence carrying a second rule or a definition** (`r73`)
228	  One sentence states one rule and holds no definition.
229	  *Ask:* Does this sentence state one rule a reader could cite on its own, with no definition folded into it?
230	    - `the orchestration law that the session keeps pulling unblocked queue work while any remains.` → `state the law in one short sentence, and put its parts in a list`
231

# The rules a human-prose audit holds a text to

This file belongs to the `text-audit` skill, whose body is [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md). That body
defines a surface and a register, and it says when a text is held to the rules below.

The rules below are the whole set a human-prose audit holds a text to. They are edited in one file,
`guardrails/language-rules.json`, in the live-spec repository.

`scripts/gen-language-consumers.py` builds four artifacts from that one file:

- the writer's page, `docs/language-rules.md`;
- the maintainer's page, `docs/language-rule-coverage.md`;
- the rule text the judging model reads, `hooks/language-laws.json`;
- the block below.

Two of those pages carry more than this sheet does. `docs/language-rules.md` gives each rule with its
examples, its exceptions, and its thresholds. `docs/language-worked-example.md` walks one short document
end to end against these rules, and names the rule at each fix.

<!-- generated:human-prose-rules — scripts/gen-language-consumers.py owns the block below -->

## The rules this audit holds human prose to

Every rule below binds human prose, which is text a person reads to understand something or to decide something. A README, a decision page, a report, a skill's own body, and a documentation page carry it. So do the prose paragraphs inside a spec. A documentation page carries `artifact` as well once it is published outside the project.

This block prints 50 of the 66 rules the source carries. A code missing from the run below belongs to a rule binding other surfaces only, or to a retired rule whose code left the set. A rule binding human prose may also bind chat, a commit message, or a worker brief. Its recorded case may come from one of those surfaces.

They are printed here out of `guardrails/language-rules.json`, which is where each one is edited. A change made in this block is overwritten by the next run of `scripts/gen-language-consumers.py`.

Each entry names the class of mistake, states the rule, gives the question to ask of a sentence, and carries one recorded case under it. The case shows written text on the left. The right side shows its repair, or an instruction where the repair depends on facts the case does not carry. Every case the class was built from lives in the rule home.

- **an ordinary word carrying a private project meaning** (`r01`)
  A word keeps its everyday meaning. A term this project needs holds one glossary entry, written in plain words. The body then uses that term unchanged, with no definition attached.
  *Ask:* Would a person outside this project recognize this word, or does the text gloss it in plain words where it first appears?
    - `The system shall red a branch whose merge-base sits behind main's tip.` → `The system shall refuse a branch whose merge-base sits behind main's tip.`
- **a coined, loan-translated, or respelled word standing where a plain standard word exists** (`r02`)
  Where the industry has a word, the text writes the industry's word. A term this project coined is replaced by the standard word, or defined where it first appears. In the reader's own language, a term is written as a real word of that language.
  *Ask:* Does a standard word already name this thing? Is the word used here that standard word, written as a real word of the reader's own language?
    - `the door` → `the entry point`
- **a name stacking two nouns with no relation between them** (`r03`)
  A name holds one noun. Where two nouns belong together, a verb or a preposition between them carries the relation.
  *Ask:* Does this name run two nouns together, and can a reader say how the second relates to the first?
    - `chat-law reminder` → `the reminder that carries the chat laws`
- **one thing answering to a second name** (`r04`)
  One thing carries one name in every sentence, from its first use onward.
  *Ask:* Does any thing named here appear under a different word somewhere else in this document or its neighbours?
    - `the mechanical checks, in the README, for the step the skill body calls the mechanical lints` → `the mechanical lints, in both places`
- **a predicate applied to a subject that cannot carry it** (`r05`)
  A verb or an adjective attaches to a subject that can carry it. Where the subject cannot act, the sentence names the actor that can: a person, a script, a hook, or a model.
  *Ask:* Can the thing this sentence names as its subject perform this verb, or hold this quality?
    - `the numbers do not show red` → `name the actor that shows a colour, or state what the numbers do`
- **a number standing with no ground** (`r06`)
  Every number says what it counts, what it is compared against, and which direction is better. A number chosen rather than derived says that it was chosen.
  *Ask:* Can a reader say what this number is measured against and which way is better?
    - `the register targets 15-25 words, and a sentence past ~25 words is a hit` → `a sentence stays between 15 and 25 words, and one past 25 is a hit`
- **a set pointed at by a count, a pointer, or a position, with its members never given** (`r07`)
  A sentence that depends on a set gives that set, or points by name to the one place holding it. A part of a set is named by what its members are.
  *Ask:* Can a person who reads this sentence alone name the members of the set it points at?
    - `**Case: the three legs**` → `**Case: the prototype-reference leg, the completeness scan, and the behaviour-traces-to-spec check**`
- **a sentence running past the word cap for its surface** (`r08`)
  A sentence stays under the word cap for its surface.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence stay under the cap for its surface?
- **a text breaking a rule it states** (`r09`)
  A text ships once it obeys every rule it states. The sentence stating a rule is the first place to check that rule.
  *Ask:* Does the sentence stating this rule obey the rule it states?
    - `a 62-word sentence inside the file that states the 25-word cap` → `the same rule in three sentences, the longest of them 41 words`
- **a thing named by denying its neighbour** (`r10`)
  A sentence says what a thing is, in its own words. A boundary worth naming gets its own plain sentence.
  *Ask:* Does the denied half give the reader anything the reader did not already have?
    - `X, not Y` → `Say what the thing IS in its own sentence`
- **an internal code leading a sentence to the reader** (`r11`)
  Plain words carry the meaning, and an internal code trails. In chat the code sits in parentheses at the sentence's end. In a document it sits in square brackets at the line's end.
  *Ask:* Does the sentence still carry its meaning with the code removed, and does the code stand anywhere other than at the end?
    - `INV-141 gives the design review a pass of its own.` → `The design review runs as a pass of its own [INV-141].`
- **a word grading how important or how good a thing is** (`r12`)
  A text states what a thing is or does, and lets the reader weigh it. A word grading importance or quality stands only beside a concrete fact.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence tell the reader how much to care about what it reports?
    - `Two constraints, and they are hard ones.` → `Two constraints.`
- **a sentence grading the person, or grading the writer's own act** (`r13`)
  A remark from the person is answered, and the answer says what follows from it. A text lets its own honesty and rigour show through what it reports.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence carry a fact, or a verdict on the person's remark or on the writer's own work?
    - `good question` → `answer it, and say what follows from the answer`
- **a sentence carrying no information** (`r14`)
  Every sentence shown to the person advances the finding, the decision, or the action. A sentence carrying a fact the reader would otherwise lose stays, however short.
  *Ask:* Does the reader do anything differently because this sentence is here?
    - `Its whole job is to mark where it stopped, what it guessed, and why.` → `deleted, since the two sentences above it already say this`
- **a word inflating a statement while adding nothing** (`r15`)
  A word earns its place by adding information. A phrase whose deletion changes nothing is deleted.
  *Ask:* Does removing this word change what the sentence says?
    - `really` → `delete`
- **the language each surface is written in** (`r18`)
  Documents, commits, code, and artifacts are written in English, and conversation runs in the human's pinned language.
  *Ask:* Is this text in the language its surface is pinned to?
    - `a commit message in Russian, in a repository whose documents are pinned to English` → `the message in English, with the conversation about it staying Russian`
- **English that reads as compressed or poetic** (`r20`)
  English in a document or an artifact reads like a native technical writer: short subject-verb-object sentences, common words, and no poetic compression.
  *Ask:* Could a native technical writer have written this sentence for an open-source project?
    - `the sketch itself carries the look` → `name the actor and say plainly what it does`
- **a word standing in all capitals** (`r23`)
  Every word is written in ordinary case. Force comes from the declarative statement itself.
  *Ask:* Is this word in capitals because it is a name the project has defined, or to make the sentence louder?
    - `CHANGES` → `changes`
- **the person an explanatory sentence speaks in** (`r25`)
  Explanatory text addresses the reader as `you` for what a person does, and names the component for what software does.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence tell the reader what they do, in words spoken to them?
    - `one` → `you`
- **a sentence with no actor, or its action buried in a noun** (`r26`)
  A rule sentence says who does what and when, in the active voice with a named actor. Its action lives in a verb.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence answer who does this, to what, and when? Does its action live in a verb?
    - `the verification of the claim occurs` → `the suite verifies the claim`
- **an opener saying what a thing is not** (`r27`)
  A sentence opens with what a thing is.
  *Ask:* Does the opening clause say what the thing is before it says what it is not?
    - `It doesn't know what a PRD is. It knows entities, states, transitions, invariants.` → `It works from entities, states, transitions, and invariants, rather than from a document's genre.`
- **a judgment with no judge and no measure** (`r32`)
  Every judgment names its judge and its inputs.
  *Ask:* Who decides whether this is true, and by what measure?
    - `broken` → `name the judge and the measure`
- **a relational word leaving its slot empty** (`r33`)
  A relational word fills every slot it opens, right where the word stands.
  *Ask:* Relative to what, by what measure, or else what alternative?
    - `a few` → `state the exact quantity`
- **a pronoun with no antecedent in its own sentence** (`r39`)
  `it`, `this`, and `they` stand with an unambiguous antecedent in the same sentence. Where none stands, the noun is repeated.
  *Ask:* Can a reader say which thing this pronoun points at without looking back a sentence?
    - `It returns the places a stranger stops.` → `That session returns the places a stranger stops.`
- **an example restating a rule that was already clear** (`r41`)
  An example earns its place by resolving an ambiguity, and it uses realistic values. One worked case per rule is enough.
  *Ask:* Could a reader have read this rule two ways without this example? Does this example stand in prose, outside a rule entry in the rule home?
    - `Grep fallback: read for the four classes by hand - sentences past ~25 words, all-capital words used for emphasis, denial frames, and adjectives that grade a result's size.` → `Grep fallback: read for those four classes by hand. The last one shows up as big, huge, minor, or breakthrough.`
- **an abstraction standing where a concrete noun would do** (`r43`)
  The text prefers the concrete noun. A required abstraction is grounded with a two- or three-item example at its first use.
  *Ask:* Can the reader picture the thing this noun names?
    - `an entity` → `A screen, a panel, a saved file`
- **a paragraph carrying more than one point** (`r44`)
  One paragraph carries one point, stated in its first sentence, with the rest supporting it.
  *Ask:* Does a reader who reads only the first sentences of this section still follow it?
    - `one paragraph carrying the author's blindness, three example defects, and the loop's origin` → `the author's blindness in its own paragraph, the three defects as a list, and the origin in a paragraph after them`
- **a long flat run of peer items at one level** (`r45`)
  A document is a tree of grouped topics, and its levels nest without skipping. A long run of peer items is gathered under headed parents.
  *Ask:* Does this level hold a run of peer items with no grouping over them?
    - `a bullet running the rule, its script, and its grep fallback together in one paragraph` → `the rule as the bullet, with the script and the grep fallback nested under it`
- **a reply that buries its answer** (`r46`)
  A reply opens with the answer: the outcome, the decision, or the finding. The opening runs a few lines, and the reader may stop there. Reasoning, evidence, and options stand underneath.
  *Ask:* Can the reader stop after the opening block and still hold the answer?
    - `a report opening with the method it ran, and the finding in its last paragraph` → `the finding in the opening lines, and the method underneath it`
- **an offer to do work the writer could already derive** (`r48`)
  A derivable act is done and reported done. A backlog item is parked for the human only after a fresh test of whether the answer can be derived now.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence offer to do something the writer already has everything to do?
    - `just say the word` → `do the act and report it done`
- **a mistake expanded into a self-audit paragraph** (`r49`)
  A mistake is owned in one line and fixed.
  *Ask:* Does this passage explain the writer's own failure at more length than the fix takes?
    - `Direct answer: yes, I broke the method... (a paragraph auditing my own failure)` → `name the fix in one line, make it, and go on`
- **a working note handed to the reader unmarked, or a choice with no open answer** (`r50`)
  Dense working notes are marked so the reader can skip them, and they carry one idea per line. Every choice offered leaves room for a free-form answer.
  *Ask:* Can the reader tell at a glance which lines are notes, and can they answer outside the options given?
    - `a dense working note handed to the reader with no mark on it` → `the same note opening with a marker that says it is a working note, one idea per line`
- **a task subject written in machine words** (`r52`)
  The harness task panel on the human's screen speaks plain product words in the documents' language, understandable at a glance.
  *Ask:* Does a person glancing at this task subject know what is being done?
    - `run gen-language-consumers.py and splice AUDIT_SKILL_REL` → `print the writing rules into the audit skill`
- **human-facing prose drafted by a writer holding the project's own vocabulary** (`r53`)
  The first draft of prose a human will read is written by a fresh writer with no package rules loaded, working from a plain brief. The brief states the facts, names the intended reader, and lists the rules binding the surface. A person who has read the rulebook then reviews and revises that draft.
  *Ask:* Was this sentence first written by someone who had never read this project's skills, working from a brief?
    - `a paragraph drafted by the session that held the whole pack loaded` → `the paragraph drafted by a fresh writer from a plain brief, then revised by someone who has read the rules`
- **a changed section shipped before two clean cold readings** (`r54`)
  A changed section is read by fresh readers who carry no project context, until two consecutive reads return zero blocking findings. `skills/text-audit/SKILL.md` defines a blocking finding.
  *Ask:* Did a reader with no project context read this section and stop nowhere?
    - `a section shipped after one reading that returned five stops` → `the section read again after the repairs, and shipped once two readings in a row returned nothing that blocks`
- **one fact stated a second time in another place** (`r56`)
  One fact lives in one home. Every other place points at that home.
  *Ask:* Does another place in this project already state this fact?
    - `the writing rules written out a second time inside another skill` → `the rules in one file, and the second skill pointing at that file`
- **a phrase the human cut returning in a later draft** (`r57`)
  A phrasing the human cut in a review round stays out of every later draft of that artifact. An approved text takes exactly the correction the human named.
  *Ask:* Has the human already cut this wording from this artifact?
    - `«X — not Y» returning in a later draft, after the human cut it` → `the sentence saying what the thing is, in its own words`
- **a defect recorded as examples with no class behind them** (`r61`)
  When a text stops a reader, the writer names the class of mistake, defines it, and enters that class in the rule home. The examples under an entry are the recorded evidence that produced the class.
  *Ask:* Does the entry state what the mistake is, so a writer can find an instance nobody has met yet?
    - `a list of banned words: leg, goes red, station, door` → `the class - a coined word standing where a standard word exists - with those four as its recorded evidence`
- **a sentence open to two readings, or hiding its cause or what it leaves out** (`r62`)
  A reader reaches one interpretation of a sentence, sees what causes what, and can tell what the text leaves out.
  *Ask:* Can a reader read this sentence one way only, name what it makes happen, and say which alternatives it passed over?
    - `it hands the text to a fresh reader who has no knowledge of its history and marks every place a stranger stops` → `it hands the text to a fresh reader who knows nothing of its history, and that reader marks every place a stranger stops`
- **a thing named by its number, so the reader must leave the sentence to learn what it is** (`r63`)
  A sentence names a thing by what it is, and its number trails at the line's end.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence say what the thing is? Does it give only a number, a position, or a count the reader must go and resolve?
    - `Requirement 233 states the orchestration laws.` → `The requirement on how work is routed between tiers states the orchestration laws [INV-241].`
- **parallel items run together inside one sentence** (`r64`)
  Two or more parallel items become a bulleted or numbered list under a one-line lead, one item per line.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence run several items together where a list would put one on each line?
    - `The system shall refuse a branch behind main's tip, a lane with no open row, a host with no worktree line, and a lane past the cap.` → `The system shall refuse each of the four faults below. - a branch behind main's tip; - a lane with no open row; - a host with no worktree line; - a lane past the cap.`
- **a rare word standing where an everyday word says the same thing** (`r65`)
  A sentence takes the everyday word wherever an everyday word carries the meaning. A rare or bookish word stands only where no everyday word says the same thing. A term of the profession stays as it is, and the words around it come down.
  *Ask:* Would a professional reader whose first language is other than English reach for a dictionary on this word?
    - `a writer marinated in this project's own vocabulary` → `a writer who has already read this project's rules`
- **a document written in the register of the message that asked for it** (`r66`)
  The register of a request settles nothing about the register of the document. A person writes a request however is fastest for them. Every document is written to the rules of its surface, whatever the request looked like.
  *Ask:* Did this sentence take its tone from the message that asked for the work?
    - `ok so the gate basically checks the counts and yells when something is off` → `The gate measures every live document and refuses a push where a count stands above its record.`
- **a defined term standing in a file that is read apart from its definition** (`r67`)
  A term defined in one home stands in another file only where that file gives its reader a path to the definition. A file read on its own carries the terms it uses, or it names where each one is defined.
  *Ask:* Reading this file alone, could I reach the definition of this term?
    - `together with the settings ladder` → `together with the four scopes that settle a setting: the session's live word, the host profile, the personal profile, and the package default`
- **a placeholder word standing where the thing's own name fits** (`r68`)
  A sentence carries the name of the thing it is about. A pronoun or a general word stands only where the name would clutter the sentence. A status word stands only where the sentence has already stated the condition behind it.
  *Ask:* Does this word name the thing, or does the reader have to carry the name in from an earlier sentence?
    - `This keeps the leading context clear enough to hold the campaign.` → `The leading session then holds enough room to carry the campaign.`
- **a step naming a check, a file, or an act with no way to run it or find it** (`r69`)
  A step the reader has to carry out names the command that runs it, or the path that holds it. Where the text can name neither, it says so and names what the reader does instead.
  *Ask:* Could a reader carry out this step from the page alone, with nothing else on hand?
    - `the structure checks over requirement shape, the generated index, the matrix references, and the frozen baseline` → `each of the four checks on its own line, with the command that runs it`
- **a set claimed whole while the text carries members outside it, or leaves members out with no reason** (`r70`)
  A claim that a set is complete states what the set covers and what it leaves out. The list printed under such a claim carries every member the claim names.
  *Ask:* Does the text's own list agree with the claim made over it?
    - `These are every rule binding human-prose.` → `the rules binding human prose, with the printed count and the reason a code is missing`
- **a claim resting on ground the reader of the page cannot reach** (`r71`)
  A claim carries its ground on the page that makes it. A file named beside the claim holds the record, and the page still states what the reader needs.
  *Ask:* Can a reader holding this page alone see what this claim rests on?
    - `The loop came from the spec-format comprehension gate.` → `what that gate observed, stated on the page, with the file that records it named beside it`
- **a number stated without the four parts a measurement carries** (`r72`)
  A number stated to a reader carries four things. They are why it is measured, what changes when it moves, its unit, and the method behind it. The four stand in the number's own sentence or in the paragraph around it. A number quoted from a named source inherits that source's method.
  *Ask:* Reading this number alone, do I know what is counted, which decision it informs, and which command gives it again?
    - `A reading returned fifteen stops.` → `name the unit, the decision the count informs, what changes when it moves, and the command behind it`
- **a sentence carrying a second rule or a definition** (`r73`)
  One sentence states one rule and holds no definition.
  *Ask:* Does this sentence state one rule a reader could cite on its own, with no definition folded into it?
    - `the orchestration law that the session keeps pulling unblocked queue work while any remains.` → `state the law in one short sentence, and put its parts in a list`

input.content:
# text-audit

**An audit-and-fix loop for any human-facing text. It runs the mechanical lints, reads the text as a stranger, and repairs the places where the stranger stops. A [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) skill.**

Point it at a text a person will read: a README, a spec section, a decision page, marketing copy, an article. It runs the free mechanical lints first. Then it hands the text to a fresh reader who knows nothing of its history, and that reader marks every place a stranger stops. You repair those places from the source material, and a new reader reads again. The loop ends when two consecutive reads return nothing that blocks a reader.

---

## Why

The author of a text is the worst reader of it. The author already holds the context the text is missing, so the author reads a meaning a stranger cannot reach. Three examples show the shape:

- a term that was never defined;
- a phrase such as "depends on the upstream state", whose slot stands empty;
- a claim whose ground lives in the author's head.

The text reads fine to the person who wrote it, and it stops a stranger cold.

The repair is a reader who holds none of that context. This skill supplies the stranger. A fresh session reads the words on the page and reports where it stopped. Each stop is marked by whether it blocks a reader or only slows one. You repair the blocking stops from the material the text rests on, and a new stranger reads again. Two clean reads in a row show that the stream of stops has reached zero.

This skill grew inside [live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec), out of a comprehension gate its pipeline held every changed spec section to: a panel of fresh readers found new blocking terms on every pass, and the terms already repaired stayed repaired. It was pulled out into its own repository on 2026-08-18 so any project can run the loop, not only that one.

---

## What it does

1. **The mechanical lints first.** Five lints run before any reader:

   - a term defined at first use;
   - a weak relational word with an unfilled slot;
   - requirement shape, where the text is a spec;
   - style and register;
   - one name per thing.

import os
import re
import unittest

SKILL = os.path.join(ROOT, "SKILL.md")
PROMPT = os.path.join(ROOT, "references", "reader-prompt.md")
README = os.path.join(ROOT, "README.md")


def read(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        return fh.read()


class TestReaderPromptShape(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_the_prompt_asks_for_five_parts(self):
        body = read(PROMPT)
        self.assertIn("write one entry with five parts", body,
                      "the reader-prompt in %s no longer states five parts" % PROMPT)

    def test_the_fourth_part_is_the_reader_s_guess(self):
        body = read(PROMPT)
        self.assertRegex(body, r"4\.\s+the guess you made in place of the missing answer",
                         "the prompt's fourth part no longer asks for the reader's guess")

    def test_the_prompt_asks_for_no_repair(self):
        body = read(PROMPT)
        self.assertIn("Do not fix anything.", body,
                      "the prompt stopped telling the reader to fix nothing")

    def test_the_skill_body_points_at_the_prompt_s_file(self):
        # The body is the reader's way in, so it names the file the prompt lives at. A body that
        # stops naming it strands the loop's second step.
        self.assertIn("references/reader-prompt.md", read(SKILL),
                      "%s no longer points at the file holding the reader-prompt" % SKILL)

    def test_no_home_still_says_the_reader_guesses_nothing(self):
        # The sentence a 2026-07-28 settlement (upstream, inside live-spec) retired. It stood here
        # after the prompt already asked for the guess, which is the drift this test exists to catch.
        stale = re.compile(r"guess(es)? no answers")
        for path in (SKILL, PROMPT, README):
            self.assertIsNone(stale.search(read(path)),
                              "%s still says the reader guesses no answers" % path)

    def test_the_skill_prose_says_the_reader_records_the_guess(self):
        for path in (SKILL, README):
            body = read(path)
            self.assertIn("writes down the guess it made in place of a missing answer", body,
                          "%s does not say the reader records its guess" % path)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
